nameStory: The 'fen' in fen crowfoot tells you exactly where to find this little buttercup – in fens, those special wetlands fed by mineral-rich groundwater. 'Crowfoot' comes from the deeply divided leaves that reminded early botanists of a crow's splayed toes, a name shared with several water-loving buttercups.
description: Fen crowfoot is a delicate, low-growing member of the buttercup family that thrives in New England's wettest places. This small perennial rarely grows taller than 8-12 inches, producing tiny yellow flowers about the size of your pinky nail. Its most distinctive feature is its finely divided, almost feathery leaves that look like they've been cut with tiny scissors. Unlike its showier buttercup cousins, fen crowfoot is a subtle beauty that prefers to keep its feet wet.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into thread-like segments that feel soft and delicate to the touch, creating an almost fern-like or feathery appearance that's quite different from typical buttercup leaves

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bright yellow flowers, usually less than half an inch across, with the classic buttercup shine but much smaller than most relatives – about the size of your pinky nail

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, sprawling plant that stays close to the ground, rarely exceeding a foot in height, with stems that feel somewhat succulent and soft when gently squeezed

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found in consistently wet areas – if your shoes aren't getting damp, you're probably not looking at fen crowfoot

habitat: Look for fen crowfoot in New England's mineral-rich wetlands, particularly true fens, wet meadows, and the soggy edges of ponds and streams. It thrives in areas where groundwater seeps create permanently moist, often calcium-rich soils. You'll often find it growing alongside sedges, rushes, and other specialized wetland plants that can tolerate having their roots constantly wet.

seasonality.spring: New feathery leaves emerge early, looking fresh and bright green. Small yellow flowers begin appearing in late spring, often hidden among the delicate foliage.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with tiny yellow flowers scattered throughout the low, spreading plant. The soft, divided leaves are at their most distinctive and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small seed heads develop. Leaves may begin to yellow but often remain green well into autumn in consistently wet conditions.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in most areas, though in protected, spring-fed locations some leaves may persist under snow cover.

funFact: Despite being incredibly rare with only 43 recorded sightings in all of New England, fen crowfoot is actually found across the Northern Hemisphere – the exact same species grows in the wetlands of Scandinavia, Siberia, and even the Canadian Arctic, making it one of our most cosmopolitan yet locally elusive wildflowers.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other small, water-loving buttercups, but the thread-like, feathery leaves are the giveaway – if the leaves look like they could belong on a delicate fern rather than a typical buttercup, you might have found this rare gem.
contextualKnowledge: The term 'fen' refers to a specific type of wetland that's fed by mineral-rich groundwater rather than just rainwater (that would be a bog). This distinction is crucial for fen crowfoot, which needs the steady flow of nutrients that groundwater provides – it literally can't survive in nutrient-poor environments.
compareHints: Unlike the robust meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup with their typical three-lobed leaves, fen crowfoot has leaves so finely divided they look almost thread-like. While yellow water-crowfoot also likes wet feet, it has broader leaf segments and much larger flowers. The tiny flowers and delicate, feathery foliage make fen crowfoot unique among New England's buttercup family members.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's buttercups, small-flowered buttercup is unmistakable due to its tiny petals - all other buttercup species have much more prominent yellow flowers.
Among New England's buttercups, hooked buttercup is unique for its woodland habitat and tiny, pale flowers—most other buttercups prefer sunny, open areas and have much brighter, larger yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercup species, meadow buttercup stands out for its tall, upright growth and deeply palm-divided leaves.
Unlike meadow buttercup which grows in upright clumps, or bulbous buttercup with its swollen stem base, creeping buttercup is the only common buttercup that spreads by runners along the ground.
Among New England's many buttercup species, bulbous buttercup is the only one with that distinctive swollen stem base.
Unlike other New England buttercups that have bright, showy yellow flowers, cursed crowfoot has tiny, pale, almost insignificant blooms.
Among New England buttercups, bristly crowfoot stands out for its rough, hairy texture and pale flowers - most other buttercups have smoother leaves and bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among New England's many buttercups, yellow water-crowfoot is one of the few truly aquatic species, distinguished by its floating stems and dramatic leaf differences between air and water.
Among New England's buttercups, creeping spearwort is unique for its simple, narrow leaves - all other local buttercups have divided or lobed leaves.

Among New England's many buttercups, early buttercup stands out for its combination of very early bloom time, preference for dry rather than moist habitats, and distinctively narrow, deeply-cut leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which grows tall and robust in fields, Allegheny Mountain buttercup stays much smaller and more delicate.
Rock buttercup stands out from other New England buttercups by having the smallest, palest flowers in the family - most other buttercups have bright golden-yellow blooms.
Among the 20+ buttercup species in New England, lesser spearwort stands out immediately because of its narrow, spear-shaped leaves – all other buttercups have lobed, divided, or rounded leaves.
Unlike the common meadow buttercup which prefers drier ground and grows much taller, swamp buttercup stays low and spreads along wet soil.
Among New England's aquatic buttercups, longbeak buttercup is distinguished by its exceptionally long fruit beaks and preference for flowing water.

Among New England's many buttercups, bristly buttercup stands out primarily for its rough, hairy texture - most other species like meadow buttercup and creeping buttercup have relatively smooth stems and leaves.

Unlike terrestrial buttercups like meadow buttercup or creeping buttercup, small yellow water-crowfoot is adapted for aquatic life with thicker, more succulent leaves and a strictly prostrate growth habit.
Unlike all other New England buttercups that grow upright, Lapland buttercup stays completely flat and creeping.
Among New England's many buttercups, water-plantain spearwort is unique for its completely undivided, lance-shaped leaves - most other buttercups have deeply lobed or divided leaves.
Unlike its terrestrial buttercup cousins that have typical yellow flowers, thread-leaved water-crowfoot has white petals with yellow centers and specialized underwater foliage.
